issues.failure_explanation: The equality analysis assumes that equality is attained (max sigma_2 = 1/sqrt(n)) and derives the three-group cluster structure; this proves only necessity. Sufficiency - that every matrix with the clustered structure actually attains equality - is never shown: one must verify that within-group pairs give rank-one (singular) 2x2 submatrices and that every cross-group pair has sigma_2^2 = 1/n. The latter is true (A^T A = I forces p*u + q*v + r*w = 0 for the group square-vectors, and the Gram determinant of a cross pair gives sigma_2^2 = [2pq + n(p+q) - |n(p+q) - 2pq|]/(4npq) = 1/n because n(p+q) >= (p+q)^2 >= 2pq), but no such computation appears. The same unestablished fact is also load-bearing inside Case A, where it is asserted without proof that the three rows representing the groups of \hat{C} form three submatrices attaining sigma_2 = 1/sqrt(n-1); hence even the proved 'only if' half (which needs Case A to be strict) rests on this gap.

failure_location.quote: The corresponding equality is achieved if and only if the rows of the matrix are clustered into three non-empty groups

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a contained lemma/computation: for a matrix with the clustered row structure, A^T A = I gives p*u + q*v + r*w = 0 for the group square-vectors u, v, w; then for a cross-group pair, sigma_2^2 = (alpha+beta - sqrt((alpha-beta)^2 + 2(alpha*beta + (u,v))))/2 with (u,v) = (r^2 gamma^2 - p^2 alpha^2 - q^2 beta^2)/(2pq), simplifying via (n(p+q) - 2pq)^2 to 1/n since n(p+q) >= 2pq; within-group pairs are rank one; since the three groups are non-empty a cross-group pair exists, so equality is attained and the three cross-group submatrices of \hat{C} used in Case A attain 1/sqrt(n-1).
issues.overall_effect: The 'if' half of the equality criterion in Proposition pr is unestablished; the Case A strictness argument (and thereby the reduction of the equality case to Case B) relies on the same unverified property of the equality family; the equality characterization in Corollary co inherits the gap.
issues.title: Only the 'only if' direction of the equality criterion is proved; sufficiency is missing and is also used unproved inside Case A
issues.why_classification: The missing direction is true and provable by a single contained computation, so no new proof architecture and no loss of content; but it is a nontrivial omitted argument - an entire direction of the main iff plus a load-bearing assertion in Case A - exceeding a routine or purely local fix.

issues.failure_explanation: Selecting two vectors from a block presumes block size at least 2, so a size-1 block yields no pair inequality at all; for a size-2 block the single pair inequality fixes only the sum |u| + |v| = 1/n + 1/p, not the individual magnitudes, and the total sum (\ref{ws}) does not fix the split (e.g. for n = 4, p = q = 1, r = 2 the data used in the argument are consistent with |x| = 6/8, |y| = 4/8 instead of 5/8 each). Hence the conclusion |w_i| = 1/(2n) + 1/(2p) is reached only for blocks of size at least 3. The missing information is already in the established block form (\ref{blck}): the diagonal entries give M_{ii} = (4/n)(|w_i| - 1/n) + 2/n^2 = 2/(pn), i.e. |w_i| = 1/(2n) + 1/(2p), for every block including sizes 1 and 2.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Read the magnitudes directly from the diagonal entries of (\ref{blck}): M_{ii} = 2/(pn) forces |w_i| = 1/(2n) + 1/(2p) for every i in a block of size p; the pair-based Cauchy-Schwarz argument is then needed only for the collinearity (u, v) = |u||v| within blocks of size at least 2, which it already supplies.
issues.overall_effect: The derivation of the equality criteria is incomplete for groups of size 1 or 2 (in particular for n = 3, where all three groups are singletons); the claimed squared magnitudes for such groups are not justified by the written argument, and Corollary co's equality characterization inherits this gap.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Then the three $2 \times 2$ matrices composed of these vectors as rows have pairwise different first (and second) right-singular vectors.
By Lemma \ref{le} vector $(\pm 1, 0)^T$ can be a right-singular vector of at most one of these three submatrices.

issues.failure_explanation: The final inference is invalid, and the lemma is false as stated. Counterexample: v_1 = (1,0), v_2 = (1,1)/sqrt(2), v_3 = (sqrt((sqrt(13)+2)/2), sqrt((sqrt(13)-2)/2)) have squares (1,0), (0,1), (2,3), which are pairwise non-collinear, but v_1^2+v_2^2 = (1,1) and v_1^2+v_3^2 = (3,3) are collinear; correspondingly the matrices with rows (v_1,v_2) and (v_1,v_3) both have first right-singular vector proportional to (1, sqrt(2)-1) (exactly: the top eigenvector of [[(4+sqrt(13))/2, 3/2],[3/2, (sqrt(13)-2)/2]] is (1, sqrt(2)-1) since s = sqrt(2)-1 solves s^2 + 2s - 1 = 0). The conclusion can fail even for the equality-case triples where the lemma is applied: group sizes with p = q + r give p*u + q*v + r*w = 0 with u+v = -((p-q)/... ) parallel to u+w (e.g. p=3, q=2, r=1 gives 1.5u + v + 0.5w = 0, so u+v and u+w are anti-parallel). What holds, and suffices for the application, is the weaker claim that the three first right-singular vectors are not all equal: if all three pair sums u+v, u+w, v+w were collinear with a direction d, then u = ((u+v)+(u+w)-(v+w))/2, v, w would all be collinear with d, contradicting the hypothesis.

failure_location.quote: Since $v_1^2$, $v_2^2$ and $v_3^2$ are pairwise non-collinear, their sums $v_1^2 + v_2^2$, $v_1^2 + v_3^2$ and $v_2^2 + v_3^2$ are pairwise non-collinear too, which finalizes the proof of the lemma.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the lemma as: the three matrices do not share one common first right-singular vector (equivalently, the three pair sums of the squares are not all collinear), and prove it from the already established orientation correspondence plus the observation that all three pair sums collinear forces all three squares collinear; in Case A replace 'at most one of these three submatrices. Taking one of the other two' by 'at most two of these three submatrices; taking the remaining one'.
issues.overall_effect: The Case A strictness argument uses the false full-strength conclusion ('at most one of these three submatrices', hence take one of the other two); with the true weakened statement at most two of the three can share (±1,0)^T, and taking the remaining one still breaks point (iii), so Proposition pr (and Corollary co through it) is recoverable but its proof as written relies on a false lemma.
issues.title: Lemma le is false: pairwise non-collinear squares can have collinear pair sums
issues.why_classification: A labelled supporting result is false as stated (with counterexamples even in the applied regime), so the repair requires formulating and proving a weakened replacement and adjusting its use; this is a contained fix that preserves all main results - more than a routine local edit, but needing no new global proof architecture and losing no substantive content.
